overview.headline: Teen saving for emergencies and early compound interest growth

keyPoints.point: Save 10 percent of earnings to build at least three months worth of living expenses for emergency needs
keyPoints.quote: save 10 percent of what you earn, and have at least three months’ worth of living expenses saved up in case of an emergency

keyPoints.point: Having six to nine months worth of living expenses offers more protection than only three months
keyPoints.quote: Explain that, if possible, it’s better to have more savings—like six to nine months’ worth of living expenses, instead of only three

keyPoints.point: Compound interest means earning interest on both the money you save and the interest already earned
keyPoints.quote: Compound interest is when your child earns interest on both the money they save and the interest they earn

keyPoints.point: Setting aside $100 every year starting at age 14 builds savings that grow with interest over time
keyPoints.quote: If they set aside $100 every year starting at age 14, they'd have about $23,000 at age 65

keyTerms.gloss: interest earned on principal and on previously earned interest
keyTerms.quote: Compound interest is when your child earns interest on both the money they save and the interest they earn

keyTerms.gloss: costs needed to cover living needs each month for emergency planning
keyTerms.quote: save 10 percent of what you earn, and have at least three months’ worth of living expenses saved up in case of an emergency

keyTerms.gloss: insured place to hold emergency savings for ready access
keyTerms.quote: Having money in a savings account can help your child avoid having to rely on credit cards or loan options

keyTerms.gloss: workplace retirement account that may include employer matching contributions
keyTerms.quote: Explain to your child that once they start a job, they may be offered a retirement account at work called a 401(k)
